## Final hypothesis (data-grounded, ages 24–32, NLSY79 1989 cohort)

**H: In this cohort of young adults (ages 24–32), age is associated with a lower likelihood of having taken more money out of savings than put in (DISSAVED = 1). The probability of dissaving is roughly flat to slightly elevated through the mid-20s (~25–26% at ages 24–27) and then declines meaningfully through the late twenties and early thirties, falling to about 18–19% by age 32.**

Direction: Negative overall — the odds of dissaving fall by a factor of about 0.96 per additional year (linear-model OR = 0.959, 95% CI 0.942–0.976, p < 1e-6). The relationship is better described as mildly non-linear (inverted-U): a slight plateau/rise until ~age 25–27 followed by a monotone decline. This curvature is supported by a significant negative quadratic age term (AGE_2 coef = −0.0085, p = 0.049; LR linear-vs-quadratic chi2(1) = 3.89, p = 0.049) and by the functional-form-free categorical model, where only the age-30, −31 and −32 coefficients differ significantly from age 24 (OR = 0.74, 0.80, 0.65; p = 0.001, 0.016, 0.005).

Magnitude: Average-marginal predicted probability of dissaving declines from 25.4% (age 25) to 18.8% (age 32) — a drop of ~6.6 percentage points over seven years (95% CI roughly 23–27% at age 25 vs 17–21% at age 32). The average marginal effect of one additional year is ≈0 at age 25, −0.85 pp at age 28, and reaches about −1.75 pp per year by ages 31–32. The observed binned dissave rate falls from 25.5–26.3% at ages 24–27 to 18.2% at age 32.

Magnitude caveat: the exact peak age is uncertain — raw rates peak at 26–27 (26.3% at 27) while the smoothed quadratic peaks near age 25; the robust, unambiguous feature is the decline from the mid-20s onward.

Uncertainty: the age effect is statistically strong overall (LR no-age-vs-age chi2(2) = 25.2, p = 3.4e-6; joint Wald test on age dummies p = 0.0001) but the quadratic term is borderline (p ≈ 0.05), the age-32 cell is small (n = 379), and the peak age cannot be pinpointed precisely. All sensitivity checks (log-income, excluding BMI > 50/60/p99) reproduce the same negative age pattern, and a multinomial model (SavedMore / Same / Dissaved) corroborates it: predicted P(Dissaved) = 25.4% at age 25–26 declining to 18.6% at 32, while P(SavedMore) rises from 30% to 55% with age.

payload.hypothesis: In this young-adult cohort (ages 24-32, NLSY79 1989), older age is associated with a LOWER likelihood of having taken more money out of savings than put in (DISSAVED=1): the probability of dissaving is roughly flat through the mid-20s (~25-26%) and then declines to ~18-19% by age 32 (a ~6-7 percentage-point drop; OR per year = 0.96, 95% CI 0.94-0.98). The relationship is mildly non-linear (inverted-U, significant negative quadratic term p=0.05) with the unambiguous feature being the decline from the mid-20s onward.
payload.workflow: Inspection of data/nls_bmi_processed.csv (12,686 rows, 0 missing) followed by: (1) descriptive DISSAVED rates by age with Wilson CIs; (2) binary logistic regression of DISSAVED on AGE(centered 28)+AGE_2(centered)+GENDER+INCOME+BLACK+HISPANIC+BMI as primary model, with linear-only and age-categorical variants for functional-form checks; (3) model selection via LR tests and AIC; (4) average-marginal predicted P(DISSAVED) profile (ages 24-32) with delta-method 95% CIs and per-year average marginal effects; (5) sensitivities: log-income, BMI>50/60/p99 exclusions, and a multinomial (SavedMore/Same/Dissaved) model. Full executable script: analysis.py; full log: analysis_output.txt.
